articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Over Two Dozen Entities in Iran's Shadow Banking Network
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced sanctions against more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aims to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks.

These designations target the financial infrastructure that supports a significant portion of Iran's remaining foreign trade, including exchange houses, offshore front companies, and the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold. The Treasury stated that these networks move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the Iranian regime with access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions.

The sanctions were imposed under Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, targeting certain sectors of the Iranian economy, E.O. 13224, as amended, a counter-terrorism designation authority, and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in various sectors of Iran's metals industry.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Individuals, Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba. The Iran designations are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and target individuals involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and recovering oil proceeds held in third countries.

Specifically, Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj were designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. These individuals are described as part of a network of regime insiders tasked with selling Iranian oil and recovering oil proceeds.

Concurrently, OFAC published new FAQs concerning Cuba, providing guidance on existing regulations. This comes amidst recent escalations in U.S. sanctions against Cuba, including the targeting of Chinese companies for the first time.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. Concurrently, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License and an amended Russia-related General License along with new Frequently Asked Questions.

The counter narcotics designations target 14 individuals and six entities tied to international narcotics trafficking. These actions aim to disrupt global drug networks and their financial facilitators.

The amended Russia-related General License and associated FAQs provide updated guidance for transactions involving Russia, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the sanctions regime. This comes as the U.S. continues to address sanctions evasion and illicit finance related to Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under its counter terrorism authorities. These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks and support structures of terrorist organizations globally.

The specific individuals and entities targeted were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but fall under the broader efforts to combat terrorism financing and related activities. Such designations typically result in the blocking of assets and prohibition of transactions with U.S. persons.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Action
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a combined action, designating entities under both its counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. This dual approach targets individuals and networks involved in activities that often overlap, such as drug trafficking used to fund terrorist operations.

These designations aim to further disrupt illicit financial flows and operational capabilities of organizations engaged in both narcotics trade and terrorist activities. The action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to addressing the nexus between these two critical threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Listings
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an update to existing Iran designations. This action involves modifications or additions to previously sanctioned individuals or entities under the Iran sanctions program.

Such updates often include new aliases, addresses, or identifying information for designated parties, or the addition of entities owned or controlled by previously sanctioned individuals. These adjustments are crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of sanctions by preventing evasion.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Iran-Related Designations to Cripple Financial Networks
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations aimed at crippling financial networks that sustain the Iranian regime. This action is part of ongoing efforts to intensify pressure on Iran's economy and its ability to fund illicit activities.

These designations target entities and individuals involved in various sectors of the Iranian economy, further restricting the regime's access to international finance and trade. The U.S. government continues to emphasize that these sanctions are designed to prevent Iran from supporting terrorism and pursuing its nuclear program.
The action follows previous rounds of sanctions under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which seeks to sever the remaining economic lifelines of the Iranian regime.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Adds Cuba Designations and Determination
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. In a significant move, OFAC also issued new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination, expanding the scope of sanctions against the island nation.

The Cuba designations include oil shippers, Cuban state entities, and Chinese military suppliers. OFAC also extended Executive Order 14404 to four additional sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.

This expansion means that the U.S. government can now designate companies and individuals operating in these newly identified sectors, creating new compliance considerations for U.S. and multinational companies with Cuba-related exposure.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations, Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License along with a new Frequently Asked Question.
The Iran-related actions are part of ongoing efforts to target fraudulent ship registries and aviation support for the Iranian regime, further restricting its ability to conduct illicit trade.

The amended Venezuela-related General License and FAQ provide updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela, reflecting the continued easing of sanctions through licenses while maintaining core prohibitions on dealing in Venezuelan and PDVSA bonds.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment provides updated authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited by sanctions. Amendments typically clarify existing provisions, expand or narrow the scope of authorized activities, or adjust reporting requirements. This particular amendment aims to refine the implementation of the Iran sanctions program.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685 Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations (URSR). The violations stemmed from the company's acquisition of customer contracts that included a blocked Russian defense manufacturer as an end-user.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) also announced a parallel non-prosecution agreement, with OFAC crediting a portion of the criminal fine against its settlement. The case highlights the importance of thorough due diligence, especially following acquisitions, to identify and mitigate sanctions risks.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, and despite having a sanctions screening process, the company failed to recognize that the end-user was blocked due to its majority ownership by a designated entity.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The violations occurred due to technical and human errors, such as channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks and failing to promptly update watchlists.

This settlement is part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, which also included a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC for anti-money laundering and Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) failures.

OFAC determined that Bank of America's apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, indicating no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation in this specific OFAC action.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based logistics company and freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations. The violations involved arranging the shipment of equipment from a designated supplier in China.

The apparent violations occurred because Pegasus failed to identify the designated supplier due to deficiencies in its compliance review and program, including screening only the supplier's new name after it had been designated. Pegasus also initially failed to respond fully to OFAC's administrative subpoena.

The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but also acknowledges Pegasus' extensive remedial measures and enhanced reporting commitments.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230
body: An individual has settled with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $1,427,230. The settlement resolves potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Details regarding the specific sanctions program and the nature of the violations were not immediately released in the summary, but such penalties underscore OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against individuals who engage in prohibited transactions.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 to OFAC
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has paid $60,764 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of sanctions regulations.

The settlement addresses potential civil liability for transactions that were deemed to be in violation of U.S. sanctions. Companies are expected to maintain robust compliance programs to prevent such occurrences.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,050,000
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington, D.C.-based global advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The settlement relates to apparent violations involving indirect dealings in the prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, an entity on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification (SSI) List.
The violations occurred when FTI Consulting issued invoices whose ultimate obligor was VTB Bank and continued to work even as those invoices went unpaid well beyond the permissible 14-day tenor.

This action underscores OFAC's focus on the economic substance of transactions, rather than just their formal structure, and highlights the importance of due diligence in identifying ultimate obligors, even when dealing with intermediaries.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Pays $275,000,000 to OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational conglomerate, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations. The violations involved causing U.S. financial institutions to process over $192 million in payments for Iranian-origin liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) disguised as Omani and Iraqi product.

OFAC determined that AEL acted recklessly despite multiple red flags that should have indicated the Iranian origin of the LPG, including third-party warnings, vessels engaging in AIS manipulation, suspicious routing, and falsified certificates of origin. The violations were deemed egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed.

Despite the aggravating factors, AEL received credit for extensive cooperation during the investigation, including suspending LPG imports and overhauling its sanctions compliance program. This settlement represents the highest OFAC penalty in 2026 to date.

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Eye Inflation Trends Amidst Geopolitical Tensions
body: Central banks worldwide are closely monitoring inflation trends, with particular attention to the impact of ongoing geopolitical tensions on energy prices and supply chains. Recent statements from major central banks indicate a cautious approach to monetary policy, balancing inflation control with economic stability.

Analysts suggest that the persistent uncertainty in key regions, coupled with fluctuating commodity markets, could influence future interest rate decisions. The focus remains on data-driven policy adjustments to navigate the complex global economic landscape.

Energy prices, in particular, are a significant concern, with any escalation in regional conflicts having the potential to trigger further inflationary pressures. Central banks are preparing for various scenarios to mitigate economic shocks.

articles.headline: Russia Warns U.S. Against 'Incautious Steps' in Venezuela Sanctions
body: Russia has issued a warning to the United States against taking 'incautious steps' in tightening sanctions on Venezuela, specifically cautioning against a total blockade of the country. The remarks were made by Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov during a visit to Moscow by Venezuelan Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.

Ryabkov urged Washington to assist Venezuelans in bridging existing divides rather than hindering talks between the government and opposition. He stated that the situation in Venezuela, including the strengthening of 'illegal, illegitimate sanction measures' and attempts to establish a blockade, would be discussed with Rodriguez.
This warning comes as political unrest in Venezuela continues, with Russia, China, and Iran having previously expressed support for Nicolas Maduro's government.

articles.headline: WHO Chief Calls for End to U.S. Fuel Blockade on Cuba Amidst Healthcare Crisis
body: The head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, has called for the lifting of a U.S. fuel blockade on Cuba, stating that shortages are severely impacting the island's healthcare system. During a visit to Havana, Tedros warned that the sanctions are endangering the lives of children.

The WHO chief announced that his organization would contribute $2 million to strengthen Cuba's national immunization program and provide essential medical equipment. The UN has repeatedly highlighted a growing humanitarian crisis in Cuba, asserting that the decades-long U.S. blockade violates international law and the human rights of Cubans.
Cuba's government reports that the measures have led to daily power outages, critical shortages of medicines, and surgical supplies.

The OCC utilizes enforcement actions to ensure that bank boards of directors and management take timely corrective measures for identified deficient practices or violations. These actions are a critical tool for maintaining the safety and soundness of the national banking system.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities to Entity List Over Advanced Computing Diversion Risk
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List. These entities, located in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand, are deemed to pose a significant risk of being involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.

The additions include MSFusion Sdn. Bhd., PT Megaspeed International, and Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd in Malaysia; Apex Enterprise Solutions (Singapore) Private Limited, Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd, and Swiftdata Pte. Ltd. in Singapore; and Megaspeed (Thailand) Co., Ltd. in Thailand. For all items subject to the EAR, a license is now required for exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) to these entities, with a presumption of denial for license applications.

This rule is effective November 23, 2026, and includes a savings clause for certain shipments already en route. The action underscores BIS's ongoing efforts to prevent advanced U.S. technology from reaching entities that could undermine national security interests.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of Commerce BIS

articles.headline: BIS Implements New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors and Data Centers
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) titled 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,' which took effect on November 19, 2026. This rule introduces new export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors, and targets certain foreign data center activities involving remote access to computing power.

The IFR imposes a new end-use license requirement for advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a 'significant volume of compute power' to end users headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination (including China). This aims to prevent foreign adversaries from bypassing existing controls by running workloads on chips located in other countries through cloud infrastructure.

Additionally, the rule establishes new destination-based license requirements for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, which BIS identifies as presenting a 'higher-than-normal risk of diversion.' The IFR also formally rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of Commerce BIS

articles.headline: Additions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 7 entities to the Entity List, under the destinations of Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These entities have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
